🌍 Iran MPs approve service fees for ships transiting Strait of Hormuz

📌 Tehran, IRNA – The spokesperson for the Iranian Parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, Hassan Ghashghavi, announced the approval of Article 3 of the “Strategic Action Plan for Security and Development of the Strait of Hormuz” during a Sunday session of the commission.

Under the approved article, ships from permitted countries transiting the Strait of Hormuz will be required to pay fees for services provided by Iran.
​
Ghashghavi told reporters that the commission continued its review of the plan during the session, finalizing Article 3, which had been pending in the previous meeting.
​
“Under Article 3, fees will be charged for services including maritime, environmental, fuel supply in special conditions, insurance, safety, and other services provided in the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.
​
The fees, Ghashghavi emphasized, will be collected from ships of permitted countries in Iranian Rials or any other currency deemed appropriate by the Islamic Republic of Iran.
​
Ghashghavi also highlighted the importance of respecting the rights of coastal states bordering the Strait of Hormuz, adding, “This plan, while recognizing the freedom of navigation in accordance with international laws and regulations, also emphasizes respect for the security of coastal countries and their sovereignty, and the prevention of violations of these rights.”
​
He further noted that the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz have their own specific rules and conditions.
​
In this regard, he cited Oman, which, after accepting the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, immediately issued a political statement emphasizing that the convention’s provisions should not violate the country’s national sovereignty and security.

California’s normal rule is that a non-urgency bill enacted during a regular session becomes effective on January 1 of the following year. So for a bill signed August 22, 2026, the ordinary date would generally be January 1, 2027. California’s own legislative glossary confirms that January 1 is the usual effective date unless another date is specified. 

AB 2624 instead makes the new protections available October 1, 2027—roughly 13 months after Newsom signed it and nine months later than the ordinary January 1 date. The reporting confirms that specific date.

What makes it noteworthy in this particular case is the rhetoric surrounding the bill. Supporters have described these immigration-service workers as currently facing serious threats, stalking and harassment. Yet the expanded Safe at Home protection doesn’t become available until October 2027. 

So there’s a reasonable question to ask:

If the threat requiring this legislation is urgent today, why design the principal protection to begin more than a year after the bill was signed?

👉 Because it’s all about narrative, not an actual law.

🚨 NEWSOM SIGNS CONTROVERSIAL “STOP NICK SHIRLEY ACT” INTO LAW

California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed AB 2624, a controversial law that critics have dubbed the “Stop Nick Shirley Act” after independent journalist/YouTuber Nick Shirley. (San Francisco Chronicle)

The law expands California’s Safe at Home address-confidentiality program to employees and volunteers of nonprofits providing immigration services. Qualifying workers who can document recent threats, harassment or violence can receive a state-issued substitute address, shielding their actual home or workplace address from certain public records. (San Francisco Chronicle)

But the controversy goes considerably further.

🔴 Under AB 2624, publishing certain protected workers’ personal information or images with the required intent to incite violence or cause reasonable fear for their safety can expose someone to civil damages starting at $4,000 plus court costs.

🔴 Posting information with the intent that someone commit a violent crime can carry penalties of up to $10,000 and one year in jail.

🔴 If the conduct results in bodily injury, penalties can reach $50,000. (The Daily Caller)

Republican Assemblyman Carl DeMaio coined the “Stop Nick Shirley Act” nickname because Shirley has been investigating and filming organizations and workers he alleges are connected to fraud involving taxpayer-funded programs. Critics argue the law could have a chilling effect on citizen journalists and fraud investigations. Florida Sen. Ashley Moody went even further, calling it the “Protect Fraudsters Act.” (San Francisco Chronicle)

Supporters strongly dispute that interpretation. Bill author Assemblywoman Mia Bonta says the legislation is aimed at doxxing, threats and targeted harassment—not legitimate investigative journalism—and the final legislation includes protections for journalists. (San Francisco Chronicle)

The timing has only fueled the controversy: Newsom signed the legislation days after Shirley was confronted outside the California Capitol by the chief of staff to a Democratic assemblywoman, who interrupted an interview while displaying a crude sign attacking Shirley personally. (MEAWW News)

Bottom line: California says AB 2624 protects immigration-service workers from harassment and violence. Critics say it creates powerful new legal consequences that could discourage independent investigators from exposing suspected fraud.

The law takes effect October 1, 2027. (San Francisco Chronicle)
